questions.question: On a dual-socket server, a thread's memory bandwidth drops sharply whenever the scheduler migrates it to the socket whose memory it did not allocate, even though the CPUs are identical. Which memory architecture explains this penalty?
questions.explanation: In NUMA, each socket owns local memory; remote memory is reachable but slower. Migrating a thread away from its pages forces remote access, so the OS must respect processor-memory affinity.

questions.question: A 500-node render farm gives every node its own RAM and disk; nodes coordinate purely by passing messages over Ethernet and share no address space. Classify this system's coupling.
questions.explanation: Independent memory plus message passing is the defining signature of a loosely coupled (distributed-memory) system, as opposed to shared-memory multiprocessors.

questions.question: Eight CPUs sit on one bus sharing a single physical address space, so a spinlock written by CPU 3 is visible to CPU 7 within nanoseconds. Classify this architecture.
questions.explanation: Shared physical memory with hardware-level coherence makes this tightly coupled: processors communicate through loads and stores rather than messages.

questions.question: A Java application on Linux must call a COBOL service on z/OS; a software layer supplies RPC stubs, message queues, and transaction management while hiding the platform differences. What is that layer?
questions.explanation: Middleware sits between applications and the OS, abstracting heterogeneity — RPC, queuing, and transactions work the same regardless of the underlying platform.

questions.question: For a satellite controller, designers pick a kernel where a file-system crash only restarts a user-space server rather than panicking the machine. Which microkernel benefit motivated the choice?
questions.explanation: Because services run as separate user-space processes, one service's failure stays contained — fault isolation — which is exactly what always-on embedded and real-time systems need.

questions.question: A periodic real-time task releases jobs at t = 0, 25, 50, and 75 ms, each needing 4 ms of execution. What is the task's period?
questions.explanation: The period is the interval between successive releases: 25 - 0 = 50 - 25 = 25 ms. The 4 ms figure is the execution time, not the period.

questions.question: A control task released at t = 100 ms must finish by t = 130 ms. What is the name for its 30 ms deadline, measured from the release instant rather than as an absolute wall-clock time?
questions.explanation: A relative deadline is the maximum elapsed time allowed from release to completion; the absolute deadline equals release time plus the relative deadline (100 + 30 = 130 ms).

questions.question: One of three replicated nodes crashes mid-request, yet clients see uninterrupted service because the surviving replicas take over. Which distributed-systems property does the deployment exhibit?
questions.explanation: Fault tolerance means correct service despite component failure — here achieved through replication and failover so the node crash never reaches clients.

questions.question: After a network partition, five storage nodes must still agree on which write to commit next; they run a Paxos/Raft-style algorithm to reach one decision despite failures. What class of algorithm is this?
questions.explanation: Consensus protocols (Paxos, Raft) let a majority of nodes agree on a single value despite crashes and message loss — the backbone of consistent distributed systems.

questions.question: HDFS stores every block of a file on three different datanodes, so reads survive machine loss and can run in parallel from any copy. Which distributed file-system feature is this?
questions.explanation: Replication keeps multiple copies of each block on distinct nodes, buying availability and read parallelism at the price of storage overhead and consistency work.

questions.question: Task A (period 10 ms, execution 3 ms) and task B (period 40 ms, execution 5 ms) are scheduled rate-monotonically. Which task receives the higher fixed priority?
questions.explanation: Rate-monotonic assigns static priority inversely to period: A's 10 ms period outranks B's 40 ms. Execution time does not enter the priority decision.

questions.question: Evaluate the Liu-Layland bound for a set of two periodic tasks: 2 x (2^(1/2) - 1). Below roughly what total utilization does the bound guarantee rate-monotonic schedulability?
questions.explanation: 2 x (sqrt(2) - 1) = 2 x 0.4142 = 0.828. Any two-task set with total utilization at or below ~0.828 is guaranteed schedulable under rate-monotonic scheduling.

questions.question: A periodic task set has total utilization 0.97, which exceeds every rate-monotonic bound. Under earliest-deadline-first scheduling, is the set still guaranteed schedulable on one processor?
questions.explanation: EDF is optimal on a uniprocessor: any periodic task set with total utilization at most 1.0 is schedulable. Since 0.97 <= 1.0, EDF guarantees it even though RMS fails the test.

questions.question: Two guests run on one host: XenGuest's kernel was rebuilt to invoke the hypervisor for every privileged operation, while WinGuest runs unmodified and relies on trapping. Which approach does XenGuest use?
questions.explanation: Modifying the guest to make explicit hypervisor calls is paravirtualization; WinGuest's unmodified trapping path is full/hardware-assisted virtualization instead.

questions.question: A carmaker's ADAS stack must keep braking control alive even if the infotainment driver crashes, so it selects a microkernel RTOS that is safety-certified and dominant in automotive and medical gear. Name it.
questions.explanation: QNX's microkernel confines driver faults to restartable user-space processes and carries the safety certifications automotive and medical systems require.

questions.question: Flight-control software must complete its control loop within 5 ms every cycle; a single missed deadline can crash the aircraft. Classify the required OS.
questions.explanation: Hard real-time systems must guarantee deadlines; missing one is total failure, matching flight control.

questions.question: Hundreds of heterogeneous machines owned by different universities contribute idle cycles to a worldwide computation over the internet. Is this a cluster or a grid?
questions.explanation: Grids span multiple administrative domains with heterogeneous, geographically dispersed resources; clusters are homogeneous and co-located.

questions.question: In a multiprocessor system, one master CPU assigns work to subordinate CPUs that only execute assigned tasks and cannot run the OS. What is this arrangement called?
questions.explanation: Asymmetric multiprocessing reserves OS duties for a master processor; SMP lets any processor run OS code.

questions.question: A file-sharing system has no central server; every node acts as both client and server. Which architecture is this?
questions.explanation: Peer-to-peer systems distribute roles symmetrically, unlike client-server architectures with dedicated servers.

questions.question: A stock-quote feed becomes worthless a few seconds after its deadline, but a late result harms nobody. Which real-time deadline category applies?
questions.explanation: Firm deadlines make late results useless (discarded) but not catastrophic, sitting between soft (still valuable) and hard (catastrophic).
